Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Pregnant women in Peru are dying at scandalous rates, according to the author of an Amnesty International report into maternal mortality in the South American country. The report, "Fatal Flaws: Barriers to Maternal Health in Peru" found that hundreds of poor, rural and indigenous pregnant women are dying because they are being denied the same health services as other women in the country. It also concluded that the government's response to tackling the problem was inadequate. Peruvian government figures state 185 in every 100,000 women die in childbirth, but the United Nations says the number is much higher, 240 per 100,000, which makes it one of the highest rates of maternal mortality in the Americas. In wealthy developed nations, only nine women die for every 100,000 births. The five main causes of pregnancy-related deaths in Peru are hemorrhage, pre-eclampsia, infection, complications following abortion and obstructed birth, according to Peru's Ministry of Health figures. Amnesty's Peru researcher Nuria Garcia said, in a written statement: "The rates of maternal mortality in Peru are scandalous. The fact that so many women are dying from preventable causes is a human rights violation. "The Peruvian state is simply ignoring its obligation to provide adequate maternal health care to all women, regardless of who they are and where they live." Garcia added: "Health services for pregnant women in Peru are like a lottery: If you are poor and indigenous, the chances are you will always lose." The report said pregnant women in Peru die because they lack access to emergency obstetric care, to information on maternal health, and to health staff members who can speak Indigenous languages such as Quechua -- a native Andean language spoken by some 5 million people in Peru. According to the report, 27 percent of deaths of women from pregnancy-related causes occurred during pregnancy; 26 percent occurred during the birth itself; and 46 percent during the first six weeks after giving birth. A 2007 Census of Indigenous People showed that 60 percent did not have access to a health facility, said Amnesty International. The Amnesty International report notes that the Peruvian government has instituted policies aimed at reducing the rates of maternal mortality, such as increasing maternal waiting houses -- rooms where pregnant women who live far from health centers can stay. Other measures include more training for health staff members on the vertical birth method common among indigenous women and teaching the Quiche language to health professionals, Amnesty International said. But the human rights group said Peruvian women and health professionals have complained that the measures are not being implemented effectively. For example, the rights group said, even though the number of waiting houses has increased more than threefold in the past eight years, only half of them are in rural areas. The agency also contends that training for health professionals on the vertical birth method is not sufficiently widespread. According to Peru's Human Rights ombudsperson, more than 45 percent of health staff last year said they had not received appropriate training, Amnesty International said. "Official initiatives to reduce maternal mortality are good news," Garcia said. "However, lack of clear responsibilities for implementing them and the absence of effective resourcing and monitoring puts any initiative in great jeopardy." Though Peru's rate of maternal deaths is high, it pales in comparison to sub-Saharan Africa, which has about 900 deaths for each 100,000 births, the United Nations says. For Africa as a whole, the number is 820. The highest rates were in Sierra Leone, with 2,000, and Afghanistan, with 1,900. Latin America and the Caribbean average 130 deaths per 100,000 births, the United Nations says, with the lowest rates in Chile, Costa Rica and Cuba. Worldwide, there were an average of 400 deaths for each 100,000 births in the year 2000, the United Nations says. The lowest rates were in Iceland, with zero, and Austria, with four per 100,000 births. The United States had 11 deaths per 100,000 births in 2005, the United Nations says. CNN's Stephanie Busari contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
LONDON, England (CNN) — Pregnant women in Peru are dying at “scandalous” rates, according to the author of an Amnesty International report on maternal mortality in the South American country.

The report, *Fatal Flaws: Barriers to Maternal Health in Peru*, found that hundreds of poor, rural, and Indigenous pregnant women are dying because they are denied the same health services available to other women in the country. It also concluded that the government’s response to the problem has been inadequate.

Peruvian government figures state that 185 in every 100,000 women die in childbirth. However, the United Nations says the figure is much higher—240 per 100,000—making Peru’s maternal mortality rate one of the highest in the Americas. In wealthy developed nations, only nine women die for every 100,000 births.

According to figures from Peru’s Ministry of Health, the five main causes of pregnancy-related deaths in the country are hemorrhage, pre-eclampsia, infection, complications following abortion, and obstructed birth.

Amnesty’s Peru researcher, Nuria Garcia, said in a written statement: “The rates of maternal mortality in Peru are scandalous. The fact that so many women are dying from preventable causes is a human rights violation.

“The Peruvian state is simply ignoring its obligation to provide adequate maternal health care to all women, regardless of who they are and where they live.”

Garcia added: “Health services for pregnant women in Peru are like a lottery: If you are poor and Indigenous, the chances are you will always lose.”

The report said pregnant women in Peru die because they lack access to emergency obstetric care, information on maternal health, and health staff who can speak Indigenous languages such as Quechua—a native Andean language spoken by some 5 million people in Peru.

According to the report, 27 percent of deaths from pregnancy-related causes occurred during pregnancy, 26 percent during childbirth itself, and 46 percent during the first six weeks after giving birth.

A 2007 Census of Indigenous People showed that 60 percent did not have access to a health facility, Amnesty International said.

The report notes that the Peruvian government has introduced policies aimed at reducing maternal mortality rates, including increasing the number of maternal waiting houses—rooms where pregnant women who live far from health centers can stay.

Other measures include expanded training for health staff on the vertical birth method commonly used among Indigenous women, as well as teaching the Quiche language to health professionals, Amnesty International said.

However, the human rights group said Peruvian women and health professionals have complained that these measures are not being implemented effectively. For example, although the number of waiting houses has more than tripled over the past eight years, only half are located in rural areas.

The agency also contends that training for health professionals on the vertical birth method is not sufficiently widespread. According to Peru’s Human Rights ombudsperson, more than 45 percent of health staff said last year that they had not received appropriate training, Amnesty International said.

“Official initiatives to reduce maternal mortality are good news,” Garcia said. “However, the lack of clear responsibilities for implementing them and the absence of effective resourcing and monitoring put any initiative in great jeopardy.”

Although Peru’s maternal mortality rate is high, it remains far below that of sub-Saharan Africa, which has about 900 deaths for every 100,000 births, according to the United Nations. For Africa as a whole, the figure is 820. The highest rates were recorded in Sierra Leone, with 2,000 deaths per 100,000 births, and Afghanistan, with 1,900.

Latin America and the Caribbean average 130 deaths per 100,000 births, the United Nations says, with the lowest rates in Chile, Costa Rica, and Cuba.

Worldwide, there were an average of 400 deaths for every 100,000 births in 2000, according to the United Nations. The lowest rates were in Iceland, with zero, and Austria, with four per 100,000 births. The United States recorded 11 deaths per 100,000 births in 2005, the United Nations says.

CNN’s Stephanie Busari contributed to this report.

LONDON, England (CNN) — The author of an Amnesty International study on maternal deaths in Peru says pregnant women there are dying at shocking levels.

The report, titled “Fatal Flaws: Barriers to Maternal Health in Peru,” says that hundreds of pregnant women who are poor, live in rural areas or belong to Indigenous communities are losing their lives because they do not receive the same medical care available to other women in Peru. It also says the Peruvian government has not done enough to address the crisis.

Official Peruvian statistics put the maternal death rate at 185 deaths per 100,000 live births. The United Nations, however, estimates the figure at 240 per 100,000, placing Peru among the countries with the highest maternal mortality rates in the Americas. By comparison, in wealthy industrialized countries, the rate is nine deaths for every 100,000 births.

Figures from Peru’s Ministry of Health identify the leading causes of pregnancy-related deaths as hemorrhage, pre-eclampsia, infection, complications after abortion and obstructed labor.

Nuria Garcia, Amnesty International’s researcher on Peru, said in a written statement: “The rates of maternal mortality in Peru are scandalous. The fact that so many women are dying from preventable causes is a human rights violation.”

She said the Peruvian government is failing to meet its responsibility to guarantee proper maternal health care for every woman, regardless of her identity or where she lives.

Garcia also said that maternal health care in Peru resembles a game of chance: “If you are poor and indigenous, the chances are you will always lose.”

According to the report, pregnant women in Peru die because they cannot get emergency obstetric treatment, do not have enough information about maternal health, and often cannot communicate with medical workers in Indigenous languages such as Quechua, an Andean language spoken by about 5 million people in Peru.

The report states that 27 percent of pregnancy-related deaths happened while women were still pregnant, 26 percent occurred during childbirth, and 46 percent took place within the first six weeks after delivery.

Amnesty International cited a 2007 Census of Indigenous People showing that 60 percent of Indigenous people had no access to a health facility.

The organization acknowledged that Peru’s government has introduced programs intended to lower maternal mortality. These include expanding the number of maternal waiting houses, which are places where pregnant women who live far from clinics can stay before giving birth. Other steps include training medical workers in the vertical birth method commonly used by Indigenous women and teaching health professionals the Quiche language, Amnesty International said.

However, the human rights organization said women and health workers in Peru have reported that these efforts are not being carried out properly. For instance, although the number of waiting houses has more than tripled over the past eight years, only half are located in rural areas. Amnesty also said instruction for medical staff on the vertical birth method remains too limited.

Citing Peru’s Human Rights ombudsperson, Amnesty International said that last year more than 45 percent of health workers reported they had not received adequate training.

Garcia said government efforts to reduce maternal deaths are welcome, but warned that without clearly assigned responsibility, sufficient funding and strong oversight, any such programs are at serious risk of failure.

Although Peru’s maternal mortality rate is high, it is far below the levels seen in sub-Saharan Africa, where the United Nations estimates roughly 900 deaths for every 100,000 births. Across Africa overall, the figure is 820. The highest rates were recorded in Sierra Leone, at 2,000 deaths per 100,000 births, and Afghanistan, at 1,900.

In Latin America and the Caribbean, the average is 130 maternal deaths per 100,000 births, according to the United Nations. The lowest rates in the region are found in Chile, Costa Rica and Cuba.

Globally, the United Nations says the average in 2000 was 400 deaths per 100,000 births. The lowest national rates were in Iceland, with none, and Austria, with four per 100,000 births. In the United States, the rate was 11 deaths per 100,000 births in 2005, according to the United Nations.

CNN’s Stephanie Busari contributed to this report.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article from London about Amnesty International’s report “Fatal Flaws: Barriers to Maternal Health in Peru,” focusing on high maternal mortality among poor, rural and indigenous women.
counterfactuals.output:
**LONDON, England (CNN) --** Poor, rural and indigenous women in Peru are dying in childbirth at disproportionately high rates because they cannot get timely, culturally appropriate medical care, Amnesty International said in a report released Tuesday.

The report, **“Fatal Flaws: Barriers to Maternal Health in Peru,”** says Peru has made economic gains and expanded health services in recent years, but deep inequalities continue to put pregnant women at risk — especially those living in remote Andean and Amazon regions.

Amnesty said the women most likely to die during pregnancy or childbirth are those who face multiple barriers at once: poverty, long distances to clinics, lack of transportation, language discrimination, and limited access to information about their rights and available services.

“Maternal death is not simply a health issue — it is a human rights issue,” Amnesty International said, arguing that many deaths could be prevented if women received adequate emergency obstetric care.

Peru has one of the higher maternal mortality rates in the Americas, according to international health estimates cited by Amnesty. The organization said the national figures mask a stark divide: women in rural areas are far more likely to die than those in cities, and indigenous women are particularly vulnerable.

Many indigenous women speak Quechua, Aymara or Amazonian languages rather than Spanish, Amnesty said, but health services are often not equipped to communicate with them. The report describes cases in which women delayed seeking care because they feared mistreatment, could not understand medical staff, or were unable to pay for transport to a health center.

For women in isolated communities, reaching medical help can mean walking for hours or traveling by river, often while in labor. Even when women arrive at clinics, Amnesty said, facilities may lack trained staff, blood supplies, medicines or the ability to handle obstetric emergencies.

The report also points to discrimination as a major factor. Some women interviewed by Amnesty said they were scolded, ignored or treated disrespectfully by health workers because they were poor, indigenous or did not speak Spanish. Such experiences, the group said, discourage women from seeking prenatal care or giving birth in medical facilities.

Amnesty called on Peru’s government to remove financial and administrative obstacles to maternal care, improve emergency services in rural areas, provide interpreters and culturally sensitive treatment, and ensure that indigenous and rural women are included in decisions about health policy.

The organization said maternal deaths are often preventable when women have access to skilled birth attendants, emergency care and accurate information. It urged Peruvian authorities to investigate deaths properly and hold health systems accountable when women are denied care.

Peru has introduced policies aimed at reducing maternal mortality, including programs to encourage women to give birth in health centers. But Amnesty said those efforts will fall short unless they address the realities faced by the country’s poorest women.

“For too many women in Peru, pregnancy remains a life-threatening condition because of who they are and where they live,” the report said. “The state has an obligation to ensure that every woman can access the care she needs — without discrimination.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a detailed news report on maternal mortality in Peru, including Amnesty International’s criticisms, statistics from Peru and the UN, causes of pregnancy-related deaths, and quotes from Nuria Garcia.
counterfactuals.output:
**News Report: Maternal mortality in Peru exposes deep inequalities, Amnesty International says**

**LIMA, Peru —** Maternal mortality in Peru has fallen substantially over the past three decades, but deaths linked to pregnancy and childbirth continue to reveal stark inequalities between urban and rural women, Indigenous communities and Spanish-speaking populations, and wealthier and poorer households. Amnesty International has repeatedly criticized the Peruvian state for failing to guarantee equal, timely and culturally appropriate maternal health care, arguing that many deaths are preventable.

According to United Nations inter-agency estimates, Peru’s maternal mortality ratio has declined sharply since 1990, when it was among the highest in Latin America. UN data place Peru’s maternal mortality ratio at roughly **69 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2020**, down from well over **200 per 100,000 live births in 1990**. Peru’s own health authorities have also reported long-term progress, although official annual counts show that deaths rose during the COVID-19 pandemic, when health services were disrupted and pregnant women faced additional risks.

Health specialists say the headline national decline masks persistent regional disparities. Women in remote Andean and Amazonian areas often face hours of travel to reach emergency obstetric care, shortages of trained staff, language barriers, and discrimination inside health facilities.

Amnesty International has said that Peru’s maternal health crisis is not only a medical issue but a human rights problem. In its reporting on Peru, the organization criticized authorities for failing to address barriers that disproportionately affect **poor, rural and Indigenous women**, including Quechua-, Aymara- and Indigenous Amazonian-language speakers.

Nuria García, a Peru researcher for Amnesty International, has warned that preventable deaths continue because basic services are not reaching the women most at risk. “**Women should not die because they are poor, because they live far from a hospital, or because health services do not speak their language or respect their culture,**” García said in Amnesty’s criticism of Peru’s maternal health system.

She also emphasized that maternal mortality reflects discrimination in practice. “**The Peruvian state has made commitments on paper, but for many rural and Indigenous women those commitments do not translate into safe pregnancy and childbirth,**” García said.

### Main causes of pregnancy-related deaths

Maternal deaths in Peru, as in much of the region, are commonly linked to complications that are treatable if care is available in time. The leading direct causes include:

- **Obstetric hemorrhage**, especially severe bleeding during or after childbirth  
- **Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy**, including pre-eclampsia and eclampsia  
- **Sepsis and infections**  
- **Complications from unsafe abortion**  
- **Obstructed labor and other delivery emergencies**  
- **Indirect causes**, including pre-existing conditions worsened by pregnancy, such as heart disease, anemia, respiratory illness and, during the pandemic, COVID-19

Medical experts stress that most of these deaths can be prevented through prenatal care, skilled birth attendance, emergency obstetric services, blood supplies, timely referrals and postnatal follow-up.

### Amnesty’s criticisms

Amnesty International has accused Peru of failing to remove barriers that make maternal care inaccessible for the most marginalized women. Its concerns include:

1. **Geographic exclusion**  
   Many rural women must travel long distances over difficult terrain to reach health centers capable of handling emergencies. In obstetric emergencies, delays of even a few hours can be fatal.

2. **Discrimination against Indigenous women**  
   Amnesty has documented complaints that Indigenous women are mistreated, ignored, or pressured to give birth in ways that do not respect their customs. Language barriers can prevent patients from understanding diagnoses, consent forms or danger signs.

3. **Lack of culturally appropriate care**  
   In some areas, women are reluctant to attend health facilities because services do not accommodate traditional birthing practices, allow family support, or provide interpretation.

4. **Weak emergency referral systems**  
   Rural clinics may lack ambulances, fuel, blood supplies, surgical capacity or trained personnel. Women with complications may be referred too late.

5. **Inadequate accountability**  
   Amnesty has argued that maternal deaths are often treated as isolated medical tragedies rather than as preventable failures requiring investigation, public reporting and reform.

6. **Unsafe abortion and restrictive reproductive health policies**  
   Peru allows therapeutic abortion in limited circumstances, but access has historically been uneven. Amnesty and other rights groups have warned that lack of access to legal abortion and contraception can contribute to unsafe procedures and maternal deaths.

García said that Peru must treat preventable maternal deaths as a sign of systemic failure. “**Every maternal death should trigger the question of what went wrong — whether the woman was denied timely care, whether she was discriminated against, whether transport failed, or whether the health system simply was not there when she needed it,**” she said.

### Peru’s progress and remaining gaps

Peru has expanded health insurance coverage, increased institutional births and invested in maternal health programs, including maternity waiting homes in some rural areas. These measures have helped reduce deaths over time.

However, rights groups say progress remains uneven. Maternal mortality is consistently higher in poorer regions, especially in parts of the Andes and Amazon, where poverty, limited infrastructure and weak health systems intersect. Adolescents, women with limited education, migrants and Indigenous women face added risks.

The UN has urged countries, including Peru, to accelerate progress toward the Sustainable Development Goal of reducing maternal mortality to **less than 70 deaths per 100,000 live births globally by 2030**. Peru is near that threshold in national estimates, but experts caution that the national average can obscure much higher risk in certain regions.

### Calls for action

Amnesty International has called on Peru to strengthen maternal health as a rights-based public policy. Recommended measures include:

- Expanding emergency obstetric care in rural and Indigenous areas  
- Guaranteeing interpreters and culturally appropriate maternity services  
- Improving transport and referral systems  
- Ensuring blood supplies, surgical capacity and trained staff in remote regions  
- Investigating every maternal death and publishing findings  
- Expanding access to contraception and reproductive health information  
- Ensuring access to legal therapeutic abortion  
- Training health workers to prevent discrimination and abuse

“**Peru knows how to prevent most maternal deaths,**” García said. “**The challenge is whether the state will ensure that the poorest and most marginalized women receive the same protection as everyone else.**”

Despite decades of improvement, maternal mortality in Peru remains a measure of inequality. For Amnesty International and public health advocates, the issue is clear: when women die from preventable pregnancy-related causes, it is not only a health failure — it is a failure of rights, equity and accountability.

counterfactuals.output:
# Pregnant women in Peru are dying from preventable causes. Unequal access to health care is widening the gap

In Peru, pregnancy can still be a life-threatening condition — not because the most common complications are untreatable, but because too many women cannot reach the care they need in time.

Across the country, maternal deaths continue to be driven by largely preventable causes such as severe bleeding, hypertensive disorders including preeclampsia, infections, unsafe abortion complications and delays in emergency obstetric care. The risks are especially high for women in rural and Indigenous communities, where poverty, geography, language barriers and under-resourced health facilities can turn a medical emergency into a fatal crisis.

The divide is stark. In Lima and other urban centers, pregnant women may have access to hospitals, specialists, blood banks and surgical care. But in remote Andean and Amazon regions, some women must travel for hours — sometimes by river, unpaved road or on foot — to reach a clinic. Even then, the facility may lack trained staff, medication, operating rooms or transportation to a higher-level hospital.

Public health experts say these deaths reflect more than medical complications. They point to a system in which access to lifesaving care often depends on where a woman lives, what language she speaks and whether she can afford transportation or time away from work and family.

Globally, maternal mortality remains a major public health challenge. According to estimates from the World Health Organization and other UN agencies, about 287,000 women died during or after pregnancy and childbirth in 2020. That equals roughly 223 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births worldwide. The vast majority occurred in low- and lower-middle-income countries, and most were considered preventable.

Peru’s maternal mortality rate is lower than the global average and far below the rates seen in the countries with the highest burdens, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where some nations record hundreds of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births. But Peru’s national average can mask deep internal inequalities. Women in poorer, rural and Indigenous areas face risks that are often much higher than those of women in wealthier urban communities.

The Covid-19 pandemic worsened those gaps. Health systems across Latin America were strained, routine prenatal visits were disrupted and emergency services became harder to access. In Peru, one of the countries hit hardest by the pandemic, maternal health services faced serious setbacks as hospitals redirected resources and many pregnant women delayed seeking care out of fear of infection or because services were unavailable.

The consequences were deadly. Regional health workers and advocates reported increases in maternal complications linked to late diagnosis, interrupted prenatal care and delayed referrals. For women with high-risk pregnancies, missing even a few checkups can mean warning signs go undetected until it is too late.

International comparisons show how preventable many maternal deaths are. In high-income countries, maternal mortality rates are typically far lower than the global average because emergency obstetric care, blood transfusions, antibiotics, safe cesarean sections and trained birth attendants are more consistently available. But even in wealthy countries, disparities persist — a reminder that maternal survival depends not only on medical technology, but on equitable access.

In Peru, advocates say progress requires more than encouraging women to attend prenatal appointments. It means investing in rural clinics, expanding culturally appropriate care, ensuring Indigenous-language services, improving emergency transport and strengthening referral systems so complications can be treated quickly.

It also means addressing mistrust. Some Indigenous women report discrimination or mistreatment in health facilities, including pressure to abandon traditional birthing practices or difficulty communicating with Spanish-speaking medical staff. When women fear being dismissed or humiliated, they may delay seeking care — increasing the risk of death.

Maternal health specialists emphasize that the solutions are known. Skilled birth attendance, timely prenatal care, access to contraception, safe abortion care where legal, blood supplies, emergency surgery and respectful treatment can dramatically reduce deaths.

The challenge is ensuring those services reach the women most at risk.

For many pregnant women in Peru, survival still depends on distance, income and identity. And as global health agencies continue to warn, a maternal death is rarely just a medical tragedy. It is often a sign of a health system that failed to act in time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a full-length international news story about an Amnesty report accusing Peru of failing indigenous and rural pregnant women, mentioning Quechua-speaking communities, maternal waiting houses, vertical birth training, and government shortcomings.
counterfactuals.output:
**Amnesty says Peru is failing Indigenous and rural pregnant women despite pledges to improve maternal care**

*LIMA —* Peru is failing to provide adequate, culturally appropriate health care to Indigenous and rural pregnant women, leaving many at heightened risk during pregnancy and childbirth, Amnesty International said in a new report that accuses authorities of allowing deep inequalities in maternal health to persist.

The human rights group said Quechua-speaking women and others living in remote Andean communities continue to face discrimination, language barriers, long journeys to health facilities, shortages of trained staff and a lack of services that respect Indigenous traditions. The report says these problems discourage women from seeking medical attention and can contribute to preventable complications and deaths.

Amnesty said Peru has taken some steps over the years to reduce maternal mortality, including the introduction of “maternal waiting houses” near health centers and training for health personnel in “vertical birth,” a practice in which women give birth in upright positions such as sitting, kneeling or squatting. But the organization said implementation has been uneven and insufficient, especially in poorer rural regions where health services remain underfunded and difficult to reach.

“Pregnant women in rural and Indigenous communities should not have to choose between giving birth far from home in an environment that ignores their language and culture, or staying in their communities without adequate medical support,” Amnesty said in the report.

The findings focus on long-standing gaps in Peru’s public health system, particularly in highland regions where Quechua is widely spoken and where communities may be hours from the nearest clinic or hospital. Amnesty said many women are unable to communicate properly with health workers because services are often delivered only in Spanish, while interpreters or bilingual staff are not consistently available.

For Quechua-speaking patients, the report said, this can mean being unable to understand medical instructions, describe symptoms or give informed consent. Amnesty said the failure to provide care in Indigenous languages can amount to discrimination and may violate women’s rights to health, equality and dignity.

The group also raised concerns about the treatment of Indigenous women inside health facilities. Some women reported feeling dismissed, humiliated or pressured to abandon traditional practices associated with childbirth, Amnesty said. Others said they feared being separated from family members or being required to give birth lying down, a position that may conflict with customs in some Andean communities.

Peru has promoted culturally appropriate childbirth policies for years, including vertical birth training intended to make institutional deliveries more acceptable to Indigenous women. Vertical birth can allow women to be accompanied by relatives, use traditional clothing or blankets, and adopt positions more familiar in their communities. But Amnesty said many facilities still lack staff trained to offer the option, while some clinics do not have basic equipment or private spaces needed to provide respectful care.

Maternal waiting houses, another key government strategy, are designed to allow women from remote areas to stay close to a health center in the final days or weeks of pregnancy. In theory, they reduce the risk that a woman will go into labor far from emergency obstetric care. But Amnesty said some waiting houses are poorly maintained, lack food, heating or sanitation, or are too few to meet the needs of widely dispersed communities.

In some areas, women may still need to travel long distances over difficult terrain, often at significant cost, to reach a facility. Bad roads, lack of transportation and extreme weather can make journeys dangerous or impossible, particularly at night. Amnesty said these barriers show that Peru’s progress in reducing national maternal mortality rates has not been shared equally.

The organization urged the Peruvian government to invest more in rural health services, ensure the availability of trained bilingual staff, expand and properly maintain maternal waiting houses, and guarantee that vertical birth and other culturally appropriate practices are available in public facilities. It also called for stronger accountability mechanisms so women can report mistreatment without fear of retaliation.

“Policies on paper are not enough,” Amnesty said. “The state must ensure that services are accessible, acceptable and of good quality for all women, including Indigenous women and those living in poverty.”

Peru’s Health Ministry has previously defended its maternal health policies, pointing to efforts to expand prenatal care, improve emergency obstetric services and adapt childbirth practices in areas with large Indigenous populations. Officials have also highlighted reductions in maternal mortality over recent decades. But Amnesty said aggregate improvements can mask persistent failures in rural and Indigenous communities.

Health advocates in Peru have long warned that poverty, racism and geographic isolation combine to increase risks for Indigenous women. While urban women are more likely to receive regular prenatal checkups and deliver in hospitals with emergency care, women in remote communities often depend on understaffed clinics that may lack medicines, ambulances or the ability to handle complications such as hemorrhage, hypertension or obstructed labor.

The issue is particularly sensitive in Peru, where Indigenous women have historically experienced abuse and exclusion within the health system. In the 1990s, thousands of mostly poor and Indigenous women were sterilized under a government family planning program, many allegedly without informed consent. Rights groups say that history continues to shape mistrust toward state health services.

Amnesty’s report argues that rebuilding trust requires more than expanding infrastructure. It says authorities must involve Indigenous women and communities in designing maternal health programs, ensure respectful treatment by medical staff, and recognize traditional birth preferences where they do not endanger patients.

The group said Peru is bound by international human rights obligations requiring it to provide non-discriminatory access to health care, including maternal care. It said rural and Indigenous women should be guaranteed the same chance of a safe pregnancy and birth as women in wealthier urban areas.

“Every maternal death or serious complication that could have been prevented is a failure of the state,” Amnesty said. “Peru must close the gap between its commitments and the reality facing Indigenous and rural women.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a CNN news article summary with dateline “LONDON, England” covering Peru’s maternal health crisis, Amnesty International’s findings, official statistics, government initiatives, and worldwide comparisons of childbirth death rates.
counterfactuals.output:
**LONDON, England (CNN)** — Peru faces a serious maternal health crisis, with poor, rural and Indigenous women at greatest risk of dying during pregnancy or childbirth, according to findings highlighted by Amnesty International.

Amnesty reported that many Peruvian women are unable to access adequate prenatal and emergency obstetric care because of poverty, distance from clinics, language barriers and discrimination within the health system. The group said many deaths are preventable and urged the government to improve services for marginalized women, especially in the Andean and Amazon regions.

Official Peruvian statistics cited in the report showed maternal mortality remained high compared with richer nations, with hundreds of women dying each year from pregnancy-related causes such as hemorrhage, infection, high blood pressure and complications from unsafe abortions. The risks were especially severe for women giving birth at home or far from medical facilities.

The Peruvian government has introduced initiatives to reduce maternal deaths, including expanding public health insurance, improving prenatal care, promoting births attended by skilled health workers, and creating maternity waiting homes near clinics for women from remote communities. Authorities have also sought to increase access to emergency obstetric care and culturally sensitive services for Indigenous women.

The article placed Peru’s crisis in a global context: childbirth is far safer in wealthy countries, where maternal deaths are rare, while women in poorer nations face dramatically higher lifetime risks. International comparisons show the burden of maternal mortality falls overwhelmingly on developing countries, particularly in parts of Africa, South Asia and Latin America, where access to skilled care and emergency treatment remains limited.
